"content": "> ## Documentation Index\n> Fetch the complete documentation index at: https://docs.mcpjam.com/llms.txt\n> Use this fi

# Evaluate

> Author test cases for your MCP server, run them ac
ross models, and gate pass/fail on deterministic assertions plus optional LLM-as-judge.\n\nA benchmark score doesn't tell you whet
her your server holds up in production. Evaluate lets you pin down the behaviors you care about — which tools fire, with what argu

ments, what the final answer looks like — and run them across the models your users actually use.

## Requirements

Evals are
available to both signed-in users and guests. Guests authenticate automatically using their guest session, so no sign-in is requir

ed to run or generate tests.

## How it's organized

**1. Project**

Holds your servers and your suites. Everything below li

ves in one project.

**2. Suite**

A group of cases plus the defaults they share: attached servers, models to run against, def

ault assertions, judge config, and argument-matching mode.

**3. Case**

One scenario you want to verify — a prompt (or a sequ
ence of prompts), the tools you expect to fire, an optional expected output, and the assertions that decide pass/fail.\n\n**4. Run
**\n\nOne execution of a suite. Produces **iterations** — one per case × model. Each iteration has its own transcript, tool calls,

tokens, duration, and verdict.

## Authoring a case

Click **New case** in the suite header (or in the empty-state screen whe
n no cases exist yet) to open the case workspace. The case is a draft until you press **Save** — backing out without saving leaves

your suite unchanged.

### Case workspace

The case editor is a two-pane workspace. The left column is where you write the ca
se; the right column shows the selected trial — a live run in progress, a persisted iteration from history, a recording session, o

r a spec preview.

**Left column — the case spine**

Every case opens in the spine, however it was authored — in the app, thro
ugh the CLI, or from an SDK suite file. The spine is a flat, ordered list of steps. Each step is one of:\n\n* **Prompt** — a user
turn the model receives. The first prompt is always present; use **Add assertion or action** to add a second prompt for multi-turn
cases.\n* **Interact** — a widget interaction (click, typing) recorded against a live widget.\n* **Assert** — an assertion that g

rades the case.

Below the step list, an **Expected outcome** field holds the goal sentence the judge grades against.

**Asser
tions**\n\nUse **Add assertion or action** to add an assertion, a second prompt, or an interact step. Each assertion row says what
it checks, who wrote it, and what a miss does:\n\n* **Route** — answers \"which tool should handle it?\" and carries that answer'
s strictness: *Reach the tool* allows extra calls, *Exact route* requires the exact order with no extras. The route is always Requ
ired.\n* **Step N** — an assertion written as a step (what the CLI and the SDK produce). It is graded in place, at its position in
the run, and is labelled by that position: a step-level \"no tool errors\" reads **No tool errors so far**, because it only sees
the transcript up to that point. Editing one rewrites that step; it never becomes a case-level assertion.\n* **This case** — an as
sertion you added here. It is graded once, over the finished transcript.\n* **Suite** — a default the suite applies to every case.
Read-only here, with a link to the suite's **Checks by stage** settings.\n\nThe list reads as a checklist with progressive disclo
sure. An off row shows only its short name. Once on, clicking the name opens an inline editor showing the full criterion, the **Re
quired / Advisory** role control, and any editable fields (thresholds, match criteria). Multiple editors can stay open at once. An
assertion that carries a number (such as a latency budget) shows it under the name at rest.\n\nA row's **role** says what a miss
does: **Required** fails the trial, **Advisory** shows the miss without failing it. The control appears when your deployment suppo
rts assertion policy; otherwise the role chip shows read-only with a tooltip explaining why it cannot be changed — for example, wh
en the assertion is inherited from the suite, or when the backend does not yet support assertion policy.\n\nBecause a failing requ
ired assertion halts the run, an assertion written as a step can leave later assertions unrun. The trial column marks those **Skip

ped**.

**The route question**

The answer here is what marks a case negative — never an inference from its steps:

* **A na
med tool** — the case must take that route.\n* **No tool should be called** — a negative case. It passes only if the model called
nothing. An assertion that requires a tool call contradicts this, and the spine says so.\n* **Any route** — the case names no rout
e and is graded by its assertions. This is a normal positive case, and it is what most CLI- and SDK-author", "is_error": false}]},
